theory.what: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is a standard protocol for collecting and organizing information about managed devices on IP networks. It enables centralized monitoring of network infrastructure: routers, switches, firewalls, servers, printers, UPS units, and any SNMP-capable device. SNMP uses a Manager-Agent model: the SNMP Manager (monitoring server like Nagios, Zabbix, PRTG, SolarWinds) polls SNMP Agents (software running on managed devices) for metrics. The Management Information Base (MIB) defines which metrics are available — organized as a hierarchical tree with Object Identifiers (OIDs) as unique identifiers. Standard MIBs include: IF-MIB (interface stats), ENTITY-MIB (hardware inventory), SNMPv2-MIB (system information). SNMP versions: v1 (obsolete, insecure), v2c (community string authentication, widely used but insecure), v3 (user-based authentication with USM or VACM, encrypted). Operations: GET (poll a specific OID), GETNEXT (walk through OID tree), GETBULK (retrieve large tables), SET (change configuration), TRAP (event notifications from agent to manager), INFORM (acknowledged traps).
theory.why: SNMP is the foundation of network monitoring. Without SNMP, you'd need to manually log into every device individually to check CPU, memory, interface utilization, and errors. SNMP enables: (1) Proactive monitoring — detect issues before users notice (interface errors increasing, CPU spiking, disk filling up); (2) Capacity planning — track bandwidth utilization trends over months to predict when links need upgrading; (3) SLA monitoring — verify service providers meet their contracted uptime and performance metrics; (4) Asset inventory — automatically discover device types, serial numbers, software versions; (5) Alerting — configure thresholds for interface utilization (alert at 80%), CPU (alert at 90%), and link failures; (6) Historical trending — visualize metrics over time in Grafana or similar tools; (7) Troubleshooting — quickly identify which interface is saturated or which device is experiencing errors; (8) Compliance — provide evidence of monitoring coverage for audits. A network without SNMP monitoring is a network managed reactively — you only know something broke when users call.
theory.how: SNMP monitoring setup follows these steps. Step 1 — Enable SNMP on each managed device: configure community string (v2c) or user credentials (v3), specify which manager IP can poll, and define what data to expose. Step 2 — Configure the monitoring server: define the polling interval (typically 5-15 minutes for interface stats, 30-60 minutes for hardware inventory), add each device's IP and community string or SNMPv3 credentials. Step 3 — Select data to collect: basic system info (sysName, sysUptime, sysDescr), interface stats (ifInOctets, ifOutOctets, ifInErrors, ifOutDiscards), CPU/memory (varies by vendor), and environmental (temperature, fan status). Step 4 — Data visualization: builds dashboards showing utilization, errors, and availability over time. Step 5 — Alerting: set thresholds (e.g., interface utilization > 80% for 5 minutes → Slack alert). SNMPv3, OID structure: 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0 = sysUptime, 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10 = ifInOctets (interface input bytes), 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.16 = ifOutOctets (interface output bytes). The MIB tree starts at .1 (ISO), .1.3 (identified org), .1.3.6 (DoD), .1.3.6.1 (Internet), .1.3.6.1.2 (mgmt), .1.3.6.1.2.1 (mib-2), .1.3.6.1.4 (private), .1.3.6.1.4.1 (enterprises), .1.3.6.1.4.1.9 (Cisco).
theory.when: Implement SNMP monitoring on ALL network infrastructure devices. Essential use cases: (1) Bandwidth monitoring — interface utilization graphs for capacity planning; (2) Error monitoring — CRC errors, input/output errors that indicate physical issues; (3) CPU and memory monitoring — detect resource exhaustion; (4) Temperature monitoring — environmental sensors on switches/routers; (5) Uptime monitoring — device reboots and outages; (6) Inventory management — hardware models, serial numbers, software versions. Use SNMPv3 where possible (encrypted). Use v2c only on isolated management networks (community strings are sent in plaintext). Troubleshoot SNMP when: (1) Monitoring server can't reach the device — check community string and ACL; (2) 'No response from <host>' — check IP connectivity, port 161, SNMP agent status; (3) Some OIDs return no data — device may not support those specific MIBs; (4) Inconsistent data — polling interval too long for fast-changing metrics (like packet-per-second counters); (5) Bandwidth utilization > 100% — counter wrap issue (32-bit vs 64-bit counters).
key_concepts: SNMP Manager — monitoring server (NMS) that polls and receives traps
SNMP Agent — software on managed device that responds to polls and sends traps
MIB (Management Information Base) — defines which OIDs are available and their structure
OID (Object Identifier) — unique numeric identifier for each monitored parameter
Community string (v2c) — shared secret password for agent access (public RO, private RW)
SNMPv3 — user-based authentication (MD5/SHA) and encryption (DES/AES)
Traps — unsolicited event notifications from agent to manager (port 162)
Polling interval — how often the manager queries the agent (typically 5-15 minutes)
64-bit counters — required for high-speed interfaces (> 100Mbps) to prevent counter wrap
SNMP Walk — sequential GETNEXT queries to traverse the OID tree
theory.configuration:
! Enable SNMP on Cisco IOS
! SNMPv2c (simple, insecure — use on trusted management networks only)
snmp-server community public RO
snmp-server community private RW
snmp-server host 10.0.0.100 traps public
snmp-server enable traps snmp linkdown linkup
snmp-server enable traps config
snmp-server location "DC1-Rack3"
snmp-server contact "netops@example.com"

! SNMPv3 (secure — recommended)
snmp-server group MONITOR v3 priv
snmp-server user monitor MONITOR v3 auth sha AuthKey123 priv aes 128 PrivKey456
snmp-server host 10.0.0.100 informs version 3 priv monitor

! Verify
show snmp
show snmp community
show snmp host

! Test from NMS
snmpwalk -v2c -c public 192.168.1.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.1  # Walk system group
snmpget -v2c -c public 192.168.1.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0  # Get sysUptime
snmpget -v2c -c public 192.168.1.1 IF-MIB::ifInOctets.1  # Get interface 1 input bytes

! Interface bandwidth calculation
! ifInOctets * 8 * 100 / (ifSpeed * poll_interval_sec) = utilization %>
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Interface Utilization Monitoring**
A core switch WAN interface shows 200 Mbps usage. How do we calculate utilization?

# From SNMP data:
ifSpeed = 1000000000 (1 Gbps)
ifInOctets at T1 = 2147483647
ifInOctets at T2 = 3006477107

# Calculation:
delta_octets = 3006477107 - 2147483647 = 858993460 octets in 300 seconds
bits_per_sec = 858993460 * 8 / 300 = 22,906,492 bps = ~23 Mbps
utilization = 23,000,000 / 1,000,000,000 * 100 = 2.3%

# Alert threshold: > 80% for 5 minutes
# Change interface speed reference if SNMP ifSpeed doesn't match real speed

**Worked Example 2: Diagnosing SNMP 'No Response'**
Symptom: NMS shows 'No SNMP response from 192.168.1.1'.

Step 1 — Test SNMP walk from the NMS:
  snmpwalk -v2c -c public 192.168.1.1 system 2>&1

Possible errors:
- Timeout (no response received): Check IP reachability (ping 192.168.1.1), check UDP 161 firewall, check SNMP agent enabled on device
- Authentication failure: Community string mismatch between NMS and device
- No response to this community: Check ACL (access-list) applied to SNMP community on the device

Step 2 — Check device SNMP configuration:
  show snmp community
  Verify community string exists and has the correct access (RO/RW)

Step 3 — Check ACL on SNMP community:
  show run | include snmp-server community
  If an ACL is attached: check the ACL allows the NMS IP address

**Worked Example 3: Trap Troubleshooting**
Link down/up traps can be used for real-time outage detection.

Configuration:
  snmp-server enable traps snmp linkdown linkup
  snmp-server host 10.0.0.100 public
  snmp-server trap-source Loopback0  ! Consistent source IP for traps

Test trap generation:
  Standby the interface: interface Gi0/1 → shutdown

On NMS: Check if trap was received. If not:
1. Is the NMS IP correct in 'snmp-server host <nms-ip>'?
2. Is UDP port 162 open on the NMS firewall?
3. Is the trap-source interface reachable from the NMS?
4. Check 'show snmp host' to verify the trap destination
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• SNMP is the standard protocol for centralized network monitoring using the Manager-Agent model
• MIBs/OIDs define what data is available; IF-MIB for interfaces, ENTITY-MIB for hardware
• SNMPv2c uses community strings (insecure); SNMPv3 provides authentication and encryption
• Traps enable real-time event notification (link down, config change)
• 64-bit counters required for interfaces > 100 Mbps
• Bandwidth utilization = delta_octets * 8 / delta_time / interface_speed

**Best Practice:** Use SNMPv3 for production environments. Implement SNMP monitoring from day one — don't wait for an outage. Set up alerts for interface errors (CRC), high utilization (>80%), and device unreachability. Use consistent community strings and document them securely.
troubleshooting: snmpwalk -v2c -c public <device> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1 — test SNMP reachability and system info
snmpget -v2c -c public <device> sysUpTime.0 — test SNMP GET operation
show snmp community (Cisco) — verify community strings are configured
show snmp host (Cisco) — verify trap destinations
Check ACL on SNMP community — NMS IP must be permitted
Check UDP port 161 (polls) and 162 (traps) firewall rules
Verify 64-bit counters for high-speed interfaces (ifHCInOctets vs ifInOctets)
snmpwalk with different community strings to test access levels

theory.what: Syslog is a standard protocol for message logging, allowing network devices, servers, and applications to send event messages to a central log server. It provides a unified, time-stamped view of events across all infrastructure, enabling correlation between different devices and services. The syslog message format (RFC 5424) includes: Facility (the source type: kern, user, mail, daemon, auth, syslog, lpr, news, uucp, cron, local0-local7), Severity (0-7: Emergency, Alert, Critical, Error, Warning, Notice, Informational, Debug), Timestamp, Hostname, and Message text. Syslog messages are sent over UDP port 514 by default (unreliable), or TCP port 514 (reliable delivery). Modern syslog servers (rsyslog, syslog-ng, Graylog, ELK Stack) can receive, parse, filter, and store millions of log entries per day, with alerting and dashboard capabilities.
theory.why: Centralized logging is essential for network operations and security. Without syslog: (1) Logs are scattered across hundreds of devices — accessing each individually is impractical during an outage; (2) Correlating events across devices is impossible — you can't see the sequence of events leading to an incident; (3) Security monitoring requires consistent log collection for threat detection; (4) Compliance (PCI DSS, SOC 2, HIPAA) mandates centralised logging and log retention; (5) Forensic analysis requires historical logs that aren't overwritten; (6) Alerting — syslog enables real-time alerts for critical events (interface down, security breach, config change); (7) Troubleshooting — during an incident, you can search across all devices for specific patterns. A 'syslog server' is one of the first things a network engineer should set up — it pays for itself the first time you need to answer 'what happened at 2 AM?'
theory.how: Syslog message structure: <PRI>timestamp hostname app[pid]: message. The PRI value encodes facility and severity: PRI = (facility × 8) + severity. Example: <133> = local4 (20 × 8 = 160 + 3 = 163... wait, no. Let's recalculate. Facility=20 (local4), Severity=3 (Error): PRI = 20×8 + 3 = 163. So a syslog message from local4.err would start with <163>. Format: <PRI>Mar 15 14:30:22 core-router-01 %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to up. Severity levels: 0=Emergency (system unusable), 1=Alert (immediate action needed), 2=Critical (critical conditions), 3=Error (error conditions), 4=Warning (warning conditions), 5=Notice (normal but significant), 6=Informational (informational messages), 7=Debug (debug-level messages). Facilities: 0=kernel, 1=user, 2=mail, 3=daemon, 4=auth, 5=syslog, 16-23=local0-local7. The central syslog server receives messages, parses them, stores them (typically in files, databases, or search indices), and can trigger alerts based on patterns.
theory.when: Configure syslog on ALL network devices and servers. Essential use cases: (1) Security monitoring — failed login attempts, privilege escalation, configuration changes; (2) Outage detection — interface down/up, reloads, OSPF neighbor changes, BGP session flaps; (3) Troubleshooting — correlate events across multiple devices to understand incident timelines; (4) Compliance — meet audit requirements for logs from security-relevant devices; (5) Capacity planning — log volume trends indicate growth; (6) Debugging — temporarily enable debug-level logging to diagnose issues (beware volume). Troubleshoot syslog when: (1) No logs received at central server — check UDP 514 connectivity; (2) Logs have wrong timestamps — NTP not configured on sending device; (3) Lost logs — UDP reliability issue, switch to TCP syslog or use RFC 3195; (4) Log volume too high — filter to higher severity levels or specific facilities; (5) Storage overflowing — implement log rotation and retention policies.
key_concepts: Severity levels — 0 (Emergency) through 7 (Debug), each with specific meaning
Facilities — source categories (kernel, auth, local0-7 for custom applications)
Central log server — receives, parses, stores, and alerts on log messages
UDP 514 (default) — unreliable but fast; TCP 514 — reliable delivery
Log rotation — rotating/compressing/archiving old logs to manage storage
Syslog-ng / rsyslog — modern syslog daemons with filtering, rewriting, and forwarding
ELK / Graylog — centralized log management with search and dashboards
PRI (Priority) — encodes facility and severity as a single number (facility × 8 + severity)
Log correlation — matching timestamps across devices to build incident timelines
NTP requirement — all devices must have synchronized clocks for meaningful logs
theory.configuration:
! Cisco syslog configuration
logging host 10.0.0.100
logging trap informational  ! Send messages severity 6 and above
logging source-interface Loopback0  ! Consistent source IP
logging buffered 65536  ! Local buffer on device
service timestamps log datetime msec show-timezone
service sequence-numbers  ! Add sequence numbers for deduplication
logging on

! Linux rsyslog client (/etc/rsyslog.conf)
# Send all facility auth messages at info and above
# Format: facility.severity @server:port
*.* @10.0.0.100:514  # UDP
*.* @@10.0.0.100:10514  # TCP (for reliability)

# Filter and send only specific logs
kern.* @10.0.0.100
*.notice @10.0.0.100

# Linux rsyslog server (/etc/rsyslog.conf)
$ModLoad imudp
$UDPServerRun 514
$template RemoteLogs,"/var/log/remote/%HOSTNAME%/%PROGRAMNAME%.log"
*.* ?RemoteLogs

# Test logging
logger -p local0.info "Test message from script"

# View logs
tail -f /var/log/syslog
tail -f /var/log/messages
tail -f /var/log/remote/core-router-01/ospf.log
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Setting Up Logging During an Outage**
A core switch fails every night at 2 AM. You suspect a link flap but nobody is around to see it.

Step 1 — Configure syslog on the switch:
  logging host 10.0.0.100
  logging trap debug  ! Send ALL messages including debug (temporary!)
  logging on

Step 2 — On the log server, monitor for link events:
  tail -f /var/log/remote/core-switch/local0.log | grep -E 'LINEPROTO|LINK|DOWN'

Step 3 — In the morning, check the logs:
  grep 'LINEPROTO' /var/log/remote/core-switch/local0.log

Expected output:
  Mar 16 01:55:23 core-switch Gi0/24: %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface GigabitEthernet0/24, changed state to down
  Mar 16 01:55:25 core-switch Gi0/24: %LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface GigabitEthernet0/24, changed state to down
  Mar 16 01:55:28 core-switch Gi0/24: %LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface GigabitEthernet0/24, changed state to up
  Mar 16 01:55:28 core-switch Gi0/24: %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface GigabitEthernet0/24, changed state to up

Conclusion: Gi0/24 flaps every night at ~1:55 AM. Likely a bad SFP or cable.

**Worked Example 2: Correlating Events During an Outage**
A user reports 'the network was down from 2:00 to 2:15.' Check logs:

Log search across all devices for the time window:
  grep '2024-06-14 02:' /var/log/remote/*/*.log | grep -E 'DOWN|FAIL|err'

Results:
  core-router-01: 02:00:32 %OSPF-5-ADJCHG: Neighbor 10.0.1.1 down, dead timer expired
  core-router-02: 02:00:32 %OSPF-5-ADJCHG: Neighbor 10.0.2.1 down, dead timer expired
  wan-edge-01: 02:00:30 %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Gi0/0 down

Timeline: 02:00:30 WAN link Gi0/0 failed on wan-edge-01 → OSPF lost neighbor 2 seconds later on both core routers → all routes through WAN lost.

Fix: The WAN link failed. Check with the provider.

**Worked Example 3: Security Alert from Syslog**
Alert: Multiple failed login attempts on a router.

  grep 'FAILED' /var/log/remote/*/sec*.log

Results:
  2024-06-15 03:15:23 core-router SEC: %SEC_LOGIN-4-LOGIN_FAILED: Login failed on SSH from 203.0.113.50
  2024-06-15 03:15:27 core-router SEC: %SEC_LOGIN-4-LOGIN_FAILED: Login failed on SSH from 203.0.113.50
  ... 50 more attempts from the same IP

This is a brute force attack. Action:
1. Block 203.0.113.50 on the firewall
2. Enable SSH rate-limiting on the router
3. Consider moving SSH to a non-default port or requiring VPN for management access
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• Syslog centralizes logging from all network devices to a single server
• Severity levels 0-7: Emergency through Debug; Facilities categorize message sources
• UDP 514 (fast, unreliable) or TCP 514 (reliable delivery)
• All devices must have NTP-synchronized clocks for meaningful log correlation
• Enable timestamps on logs: 'service timestamps log datetime msec'
• Syslog is essential for security monitoring, troubleshooting, and compliance

**Best Practice:** Configure syslog on every device during initial setup. Use TCP syslog for critical devices (core routers, firewalls). Filter messages to appropriate severity — start with 'informational' (6) and only use 'debug' (7) temporarily. Set up alerts for severity 0-3 messages. Archive logs with rotation and retain for at least 90 days (or as required by compliance).
troubleshooting: show logging (Cisco) — view log buffer and verify syslog destination
tail -f /var/log/syslog — monitor incoming syslog messages on server
logger -p local0.info "Test message" — send test syslog message
Check UDP 514/TCP 514 connectivity between device and log server
Verify NTP sync on all devices — wrong timestamps = useless logs
Check log rotation — ensure disk doesn't fill up
Filter noisy messages to reduce storage requirements
TCP syslog vs UDP: TCP is reliable but may block if server is unreachable

theory.what: NetFlow is a network protocol developed by Cisco for collecting IP traffic flow information. A flow is defined as a unidirectional sequence of packets sharing: Source IP, Destination IP, Source Port, Destination Port, Layer 3 Protocol Type, Type of Service (ToS), and Input Interface. NetFlow captures metadata about every flow — who is talking to whom, on which ports, how much data, and for how long — without capturing the actual packet payloads. This makes it far more storage-efficient than full packet capture. Versions: NetFlow v5 (fixed-format, widely supported), NetFlow v9 (template-based, flexible fields), IPFIX (standardized NetFlow v10, RFC 7011), and sFlow (sampled flow export, less CPU overhead). The exporter (router/switch) sends flow records to a collector (nfdump, ntopng, PRTG, SolarWinds) which aggregates and visualizes the data. Key metrics per flow: start/end timestamps, byte count, packet count, and TCP flags.
theory.why: NetFlow provides visibility that SNMP and syslog alone cannot deliver. While SNMP shows interface utilization ('how much traffic'), NetFlow answers the much richer question ('which traffic?'). Key benefits: (1) Traffic analysis — identify top talkers, top applications, and bandwidth consumption by host; (2) Security monitoring — detect DDoS attacks, botnet traffic, data exfiltration, and C2 communication; (3) Capacity planning — understand bandwidth usage patterns by application, user, and time of day; (4) Billing/chargeback — measure bandwidth usage per department or customer; (5) Troubleshooting — identify traffic spikes and which hosts/applications caused them; (6) Compliance — demonstrate traffic segmentation and access control enforcement; (7) NetFlow enables hunting lateral movement: an internal host sending SSH traffic to an external IP is suspicious but invisible without flow data. Network engineers who deploy NetFlow gain superpowers that SNMP-only engineers lack.
theory.how: NetFlow operation: Step 1 — The router/switch inspects packets and builds a flow cache. A new flow entry is created for the first packet with a unique 5-tuple (src IP, dst IP, src port, dst port, protocol). Step 2 — Subsequent matching packets update the flow record (packet count, byte count, timestamp). Step 3 — Various conditions trigger flow export: the flow ends (TCP FIN/RST), the flow is idle for a configured timeout (default 30s), the flow is active for the maximum timeout (default 30min), or the flow cache is full. Step 4 — The exporter sends flow records to the collector using UDP (typically port 2055). Step 5 — The collector parses, aggregates, stores, and visualizes the flow data. NetFlow v5 records have a fixed format (no flexibility), while v9 and IPFIX use templates allowing the exporter to define which fields to include. sFlow differs by performing statistical sampling (e.g., 1 in 1000 packets) rather than complete flow accounting — this reduces CPU impact but loses some accuracy. nfdump is a common open-source tool for NetFlow analysis: 'nfdump -R /data/nfcapd/ -s ip/flows' lists top IPs by flows.
theory.when: Enable NetFlow on key network segments: (1) WAN edges — internet and site-to-site links (discover bandwidth hogging applications); (2) Internet gateways — monitor for DDoS attacks and data exfiltration; (3) Core switches — track traffic between network segments; (4) Data center uplinks — understand east-west traffic patterns; (5) Server access ports — track specific server traffic profiles; (6) Security zones — monitor traffic crossing zone boundaries. Troubleshoot NetFlow when: (1) Collector shows no data — check NetFlow export configuration; (2) Data seems incomplete — sampling rate too high or export timeout too long; (3) High CPU on exporter — reduce sampling rate or move to hardware-accelerated flow; (4) Storage growing too fast — adjust export timeout or aggregate at the collector; (5) IPFIX templates not matching — exporter and collector template configuration mismatch.
key_concepts: Flow — unidirectional sequence of packets sharing 5-tuple (src/dst IP, src/dst port, protocol)
NetFlow v5 — fixed-format flow export, widely supported, limited fields
NetFlow v9 — template-based, flexible fields, supports custom exporter configurations
IPFIX (NetFlow v10) — standardized flow export protocol (RFC 7011, RFC 5101)
sFlow — sampled flow export (1:N packets), lower CPU, statistical accuracy
Collector — receives and processes flow records (nfdump, ntopng, PRTG, SolarWinds)
Exporter — router/switch generating and sending flow records
Flow cache — router's internal table of active flows, built from packet inspection
Sampling — recording only 1 of every N packets (reduces CPU, affects accuracy)
Top talkers — highest-traffic hosts or applications identified from flow data
theory.configuration:
! Cisco NetFlow v5 (traditional, simple)
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip route-cache flow
! Export flow data to collector
ip flow-export destination 10.0.0.100 2055
ip flow-export version 5

! Cisco NetFlow v9 (flexible, recommended)
flow exporter EXPORTER-1
 destination 10.0.0.100
 transport udp 2055
 source Loopback0
 export-protocol netflow-v9
!
flow monitor MONITOR-1
 exporter EXPORTER-1
 record netflow ipv4 original-input
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip flow monitor MONITOR-1 input
 ip flow monitor MONITOR-1 output
!
! sFlow (on Arista/HPE/Extreme)
sflow enable
sflow destination 10.0.0.100 6343
sflow sample 1000  ! Sample 1 in 1000 packets
sflow polling-interval 30

! Verify
show flow exporter EXPORTER-1
show flow monitor MONITOR-1
show ip cache flow  ! NetFlow v5 active flows

! nfdump analysis commands
nfdump -R /data/nfcapd/ -s ip/flows -n 10  # Top 10 source IPs by flows
nfdump -R /data/nfcapd/ -s ip/bytes -n 10  # Top 10 source IPs by bytes
nfdump -R /data/nfcapd/ 'proto tcp and port 443'  # Filter by protocol/port
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Identifying Bandwidth Hogs**
A WAN link is saturated. SNMP shows 95% utilization but doesn't tell you what's using it.

NetFlow query: 'nfdump -R /data/nfcapd/ -s ip/bytes -n 10'

Results:
  Top 10 Source IPs (bytes):
  1.  10.0.1.100     (Office365 backup)   500 GB
  2.  10.0.2.50      (YouTube user)       200 GB
  3.  10.0.1.200     (Windows Update)     150 GB

Non-critical traffic is consuming the bandwidth. Action:
1. Shape/shcedule Office365 backup to off-peak hours
2. Block/rate-limit YouTube at the firewall
3. Schedule Windows Updates to business hours or use local WSUS

**Worked Example 2: Detecting a DDoS Attack**
Symptom: External link saturated, legitimate users can't access services.

NetFlow query: 'nfdump -R /data/nfcapd/ 'not dst net 203.0.113.0/24 and not src net 10.0.0.0/8' -s ip/flows -n 10 | head -20'

Results:
  10.0.0.1:80 (web server) receiving SYN packets from thousands of different IPs

Analysis: SYN flood DDoS attack against the web server. Each source IP sends a few SYN packets but never completes the handshake.

Mitigation:
1. Enable SYN cookies on the web server
2. Rate-limit incoming SYN packets at the firewall
3. Deploy DDoS protection (AWS Shield, Cloudflare, Arbor)
4. Use BGP Flowspec to drop the attack traffic

**Worked Example 3: Investigating Possible Data Exfiltration**
Alert: Internal database server (10.0.0.50) sending large amounts of data to external IP 5.5.5.5.

NetFlow query: 'nfdump -R /data/nfcapd/ 'src ip 10.0.0.50'

Results:
  10.0.0.50:3306 → 5.5.5.5:443    873 MB    Duration: 03:00:00

An internal MySQL database sending 873 MB to an external server over port 443 (HTTPS). This is abnormal.

Action: Investigate immediately. If this host doesn't normally connect to 5.5.5.5, it could be a data breach. Block the connection at the firewall and conduct forensic analysis.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• NetFlow captures flow metadata (who talks to whom, on which ports, how much data) without packet payloads
• NetFlow v5 (fixed), v9 (flexible templates), and IPFIX (standardized v10) are the main versions
• sFlow uses statistical sampling for lower CPU impact
• Essential for: bandwidth analysis, security monitoring, capacity planning, and traffic troubleshooting
• nfdump is the standard open-source tool for NetFlow analysis
• Export to collector on UDP 2055 (configurable)

**Best Practice:** Enable NetFlow v9 or IPFIX on WAN edges, internet gateways, and core switches. Configure appropriate export timeouts (30s idle, 30min active). Use 64-bit counters for high-speed interfaces. Store flow records for at least 30 days for trending and incident response.
troubleshooting: show flow exporter — verify export statistics (exported flows, errors)
show flow monitor — check flows being monitored and exported
show ip cache flow — view active flow cache (NetFlow v5)
Check connectivity: can the exporter reach the collector (UDP 2055)?
Verify flow monitor is applied to the correct interface and direction (input/output)
High CPU: increase sampling rate or use hardware-accelerated NetFlow
No data: check 'show flow monitor' cache is building; check collector configuration
Use nfdump/nfcapd for debugging: nfcapd -l /tmp/test -p 2055 (run in foreground)

theory.what: Network troubleshooting is the systematic process of identifying, isolating, and resolving network problems. The key word is 'systematic' — without a structured methodology, troubleshooting becomes random guesswork that wastes time and often misses the root cause. The most common approach is the OSI model-based method, where you check each layer from bottom to top (Physical → Data Link → Network → Transport → Application). This ensures you don't waste time checking application configuration when the cable is unplugged. An alternative is the 'divide and conquer' method — start at Layer 3 (ping), and depending on the result, go up or down the stack. The key rule of troubleshooting: ALWAYS start by asking 'What changed?' — most network issues are caused by a recent change, not spontaneous failure. Other critical principles: (1) Isolate the problem — determine if it's one device, one subnet, or the entire network; (2) Reproduce the issue — can you make it happen reliably?; (3) Check the obvious first — cable plugged in? Power on? IP configured?; (4) Document what you find — this helps if you escalate; (5) One change at a time — making multiple changes simultaneously hides the real fix.
theory.why: A structured troubleshooting methodology is essential because: (1) It reduces MTTR (Mean Time to Resolution) — following a systematic approach is faster than random guessing; (2) It prevents missed causes — the OSI model ensures you check every layer; (3) It provides a common language — 'I checked Layer 3 and L3 is fine, it's an L4 problem' communicates precisely; (4) It enables delegation — you can hand off specific steps to different team members; (5) It reduces finger-pointing — systematic evidence shows where the problem actually is; (6) It builds institutional knowledge — documented troubleshooting flows help new team members. The 'What changed?' question alone saves countless hours. Most network outages are caused by a recent change — a new ACL, a routing change, a firmware upgrade. If nobody changed anything, then the problem is likely hardware failure. Without methodology, experienced engineers rely on intuition that junior engineers lack. With methodology, anyone can follow the same steps.
theory.how: The systematic troubleshooting process follows these steps. Step 1 — Define the problem: What exactly is the symptom? One user can't access the internet? Or the entire office is down? When did it start? Did anything change? Step 2 — Gather information: Check the tools — monitoring alerts, status dashboards, recent change tickets, helpdesk reports. Step 3 — Isolate the scope: Is it one device (client-side), one subnet (network segmentation), one application (server-side), multiple devices (shared infrastructure)? Step 4 — Apply the OSI model: Layer 1 (Physical) — cable plugged in, link light on? Check 'show interfaces status' for up/up, no errors. Layer 2 (Data Link) — MAC table populated, VLAN correct, STP not blocking? Check 'show mac address-table', 'show vlan', 'show spanning-tree'. Layer 3 (Network) — IP address configured correctly, subnet mask matches, default gateway set? Check 'ping <gateway>', 'show ip interface', 'show ip route'. Layer 4 (Transport) — Port reachable, firewall not blocking? Check 'nc -zv host port', 'show access-list'. Layer 7 (Application) — Service running, DNS resolving? Check 'systemctl status service', 'nslookup domain'. Step 5 — Develop a hypothesis: Based on the evidence, what's the most likely cause? Step 6 — Test the hypothesis: Make one change to test. Did the problem resolve? Step 7 — Implement the fix: Apply the permanent solution. Step 8 — Document: Record the problem, diagnosis, and solution for future reference.
theory.when: Use this methodology for ANY network problem — from 'My email isn't working' to 'The entire data center is down'. Specific scenarios where systematic troubleshooting is critical: (1) Intermittent problems — the hardest to diagnose, requiring logging and patience; (2) Problems that span multiple teams (networking, security, application) — objective data cuts through finger-pointing; (3) High-severity incidents — panic leads to random changes; methodology keeps you focused; (4) Problems in unfamiliar environments — methodology tells you what to check even if you don't know the specific hardware; (5) Escalations — when you hand off to a senior engineer, documented methodology shows what you've already eliminated.
key_concepts: OSI-based approach — start at L1 and work up (cable → switching → routing → firewall → application)
Divide and conquer — start at L3 (ping), go up/down based on result
What changed? — the single most important troubleshooting question
Isolate the scope — one device, subnet, application, or entire network?
One change at a time — make a single change, test, then move to the next
Document everything — you can't remember details under pressure
Check the obvious first — cables, power, IP configuration, firewall rules
Bottleneck principle — find the slowest component in the path
Deflection testing — swap a known-good component (cable, port, device) to isolate
Binary search — test the midpoint of a path to quickly locate the problem

# Quick diagnostic toolkit sequence
echo "=== Layer 1-2 Check ==="
ip link show eth0  | grep state  # Interface up?
ip addr show eth0 | grep inet   # IP configured?

echo "=== Layer 3 Check ==="
ping -c 2 192.168.1.1              # Can I reach the gateway?
ping -c 2 8.8.8.8                  # Can I reach the internet?
traceroute -n 8.8.8.8              # Where does the path break?

echo "=== Layer 4 Check ==="
nc -zv -w 3 8.8.8.8 53             # DNS port reachable?
nc -zv -w 3 google.com 443        # HTTPS reachable?

echo "=== Layer 7 Check ==="
nslookup google.com               # DNS resolution working?
curl -v -o /dev/null https://google.com  # Full HTTP test

echo "=== Local State ==="
ss -tlnp                           # Listening services
ss -tan | head -20                 # Active connections
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: 'Internet is Down'**
A user says 'the internet is down'. Follow methodology:

Step 1 — Define the problem: One user or everyone? Just this user → client-side. Everyone → likely shared infrastructure.
Step 2 — Check: Can you reach the gateway? (ping 192.168.1.1 → works).
Step 3 — Can you reach beyond the gateway? (ping 8.8.8.8 → fails).
Step 4 — Check the edge router: show ip route 0.0.0.0 → default route exists.
Step 5 — Check the WAN interface: show ip interface brief → WAN IP shows up/up.
Step 6 — Is the ISP reachable? ping ISP next-hop → fails.
Step 7 — Check the ISP connection: show interfaces Serial0/0/0 → Input errors: 5000.
Step 8 — Conclusion: WAN link is up but has excessive errors. Likely a bad circuit or CSU/DSU issue.

Escalate to ISP with evidence.

**Worked Example 2: Intermittent Video Conferencing Problems**
Users report that video calls freeze periodically.

Step 1 — Reproduce: Join a video call and monitor network conditions.
Step 2 — Check: Is the problem specific to one conference room or all rooms? All rooms → infrastructure issue.
Step 3 — Continuous ping during a call: ping gateway → some packets drop (2% loss).
Step 4 — Check interfaces: show interfaces → CRC errors incrementing on the call's VLAN switch port.
Step 5 — Check cable: Reseat the cable, CRC errors stop. Problem solved.

Root cause: Bad cable causing intermittent CRC errors, which TCP recovers from but real-time video can't (UDP).

**Worked Example 3: 'Can't Reach Email Server'**
User can't connect to the company email server.

Step 1 — Isolate: Can other users reach the email server? Yes → client-side. No → server-side.
Step 2 — Client-side check: ping mail.example.com → resolves but timed out.
Step 3 — No wait, ping IP: ping 10.0.0.10 (email server IP) → works.
Step 4 — Test port: nc -zv 10.0.0.10 143 (IMAP) → Connection refused.
Step 5 — Check on server: systemctl status dovecot → service not running.
Step 6 — Start the service: systemctl start dovecot → problem resolved.

Root cause: Email service stopped. By isolating the scope and checking systematically, we identified it's a server-side application issue, not a network problem.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• Use the OSI model systematically: L1 (cable/link) → L2 (switch/MAC/VLAN) → L3 (IP/routing) → L4 (port/firewall) → L7 (application)
• Always ask 'What changed?' — most outages are caused by changes
• Isolate scope: one device → client; entire subnet → infrastructure; multiple locations → WAN
• One change at a time — making multiple changes hides the real fix
• Document everything — you'll forget under pressure, and documentation helps escalation
• Check the obvious first — cables, power, IP configuration, 'did you reboot?'

**Best Practice:** Create a standard troubleshooting checklist and use it consistently. Document every incident with the problem, diagnosis, and resolution. Build a knowledge base of common issues and their symptoms for faster resolution in the future.
troubleshooting: Step 1: ping <gateway> — L3 basic connectivity test
Step 2: ping <remote_ip> — beyond the gateway
Step 3: nslookup <domain> — DNS resolution (L7)
Step 4: nc -zv <host> <port> — TCP port connectivity (L4)
Step 5: traceroute <dest> — path analysis
Step 6: check 'show interfaces' for errors, speed/duplex
Step 7: check 'show running-config' for recent changes
Step 8: What changed? Ask the team, check change tickets, check git logs

theory.what: Capacity planning is the process of monitoring current resource utilization, analyzing growth trends, and predicting when infrastructure upgrades will be needed to prevent performance degradation or outages. It covers all network resources: bandwidth (WAN links, internet circuits, inter-switch links), device processing capacity (CPU, memory on routers and switches), storage (log servers, monitoring databases, backups), and power/environmental (UPS capacity, cooling, rack space). The core methodology involves: establishing a baseline (measure current utilization — average, peak, and 95th percentile), trending (analyze growth rates over weeks to months), forecasting (project when utilization will exceed capacity thresholds), and planning (budget and schedule upgrades before hitting limits). Key thresholds: 70% (monitor, plan for upgrade within 6-12 months), 80% (escalate, plan upgrade within 3 months), 90% (critical, implement upgrade as soon as possible). Without capacity planning, you will run out of bandwidth at the worst possible time — during a critical business period when spending money under pressure is expensive and stressful.
theory.why: Capacity planning prevents reactive, expensive emergency upgrades. Without it: (1) WAN links saturate during peak business hours, slowing critical applications; (2) Storage fills up, causing log loss or system crashes; (3) SNMP polling fails because the monitoring server is out of memory; (4) Emergency hardware shipping costs a premium vs planned procurement; (5) Network upgrades happen during business hours (emergency) vs scheduled maintenance windows; (6) Budget surprises — CFOs hate unplanned capital expenditures; (7) SLA violations — saturated links cause packet loss and jitter, violating voice/video SLAs. Proactive capacity planning transforms IT from a 'break-fix' operation to a strategic partner that enables business growth. The 95th percentile method is standard: you collect utilization data every 5 minutes for a month, sort the values, and take the value at 95% (discarding the top 5% of peaks). This avoids planning for unrealistic spikes while still capturing sustained peak usage.
theory.how: Capacity planning process: Step 1 — Data Collection: Collect interface utilization (SNMP ifInOctets/ifOutOctets), CPU/memory stats, and storage usage. Poll intervals: 5 minutes for interfaces, 15 minutes for CPU/memory, hourly for storage. Step 2 — Baselines: For each resource, record the average utilization (typical load), peak utilization (busiest period), and 95th percentile (sustained peak, discarding brief spikes). Note the time-of-day and day-of-week patterns. Step 3 — Trend Analysis: Compare current metrics against historical data. Calculate growth rate: (current utilization - historical utilization) / time_period. Is growth linear, exponential, or seasonal? Step 4 — Forecasting: Project when utilization will exceed capacity at current growth rates. 'At 5% monthly growth, the 100 Mbps WAN link will exceed 80% utilization in 4 months.' Step 5 — Budgeting and Procurement: Document planned upgrades with timeline and budget estimates. Include lead time for procurement (30-90 days for hardware) and installation. Step 6 — Implementation: Schedule upgrades during maintenance windows. Implement the upgrade. Update baseline documentation with new capacity. Granularity matters: daily averages hide peak-hour saturation. Always examine 5-minute or 15 minute intervals for accurate utilization data. CRM integration: capacity plan should link to procurement system for automated PO generation when thresholds are crossed.
theory.when: Review capacity data monthly, report to management quarterly. Monitor for these escalation triggers: (1) Interface utilization consistently above 70% — add to watch list; (2) Interface utilization above 80% for 2 consecutive weeks — plan upgrade; (3) Interface utilization above 90% — urgent upgrade needed; (4) CPU above 75% on core devices — investigate and plan upgrades; (5) Memory utilization increasing (memory leak) — investigate root cause; (6) Storage trending to full within 3 months — archive or expand; (7) Snmp polling failure rate increasing — monitoring server capacity exceeded. Common capacity pitfalls: (1) Planning based on average utilization (hides peak usage); (2) Forgetting that bandwidth grows (new applications, more users); (3) Not monitoring both directions (asymmetric links); (4) Assuming hardware lasts forever (5-year refresh cycle recommended); (5) Ignoring seasonal patterns (holiday spikes, end-of-month billing).
key_concepts: Baseline — current utilization metrics (average, peak, 95th percentile)
95th percentile — utilization representing sustained peak (discards top 5% spikes)
Growth trending — calculating the rate of utilization increase over time
Thresholds — 70% (watch), 80% (plan), 90% (act now)
Lead time — time required to procure and install upgrades (30-90 days for hardware)
Seasonal patterns — predictable utilization variations (holiday, month-end, quarterly)
Oversubscription — ratio of aggregate capacity to total potential demand (e.g., 20:1 for access layer)
SNMP polling — collecting interface utilization stats (5-min intervals recommended)
NetFlow for application bandwidth — which apps are consuming the capacity?
Refresh cycle — replace hardware every 5 years to maintain vendor support and performance

theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: WAN Link Capacity Planning**
A 100 Mbps WAN link has the following utilization data:
- January: avg 40 Mbps, peak 75 Mbps
- February: avg 42 Mbps, peak 78 Mbps
- March: avg 44 Mbps, peak 81 Mbps
- April: avg 46 Mbps, peak 84 Mbps

Growth rate: 2 Mbps/month (8% annually)
Current peak: 84 Mbps (84% of capacity — ABOVE 80% threshold!)

Forecast: At 2 Mbps/month growth, peak will hit 90 Mbps (90%) in 3 months, and 100 Mbps (100%) in 8 months.

Recommendation: Order upgrade to 200 Mbps immediately (90-day lead time).
Without action: In 3 months, sustained peak will exceed 90% utilization, causing congestion, packet loss, and application degradation.

**Worked Example 2: Data Center Uplink Planning**
A 4 × 10 Gbps EtherChannel (40 Gbps aggregate) between ToR and Leaf switches.

Current utilization: 30 Gbps peak (75% of 40 Gbps)
Growth rate: 20% year-over-year

Time to 80% threshold: Current 75%. At 20% YoY growth, utilization increases to 80% in approximately 4 months.

Options:
1. Add 2 more 10 Gbps links to the bundle (simple, no hardware change)
2. Upgrade to 25 Gbps links (requires new SFPs and possibly new switches)
3. Add another bundle for specific traffic types

**Worked Example 3: 95th Percentile Billing Analysis**
An ISP bills based on 95th percentile utilization. Understanding this helps control costs.

The 95th percentile: Collect 5-minute samples for a month (8640 samples). Sort them. The 95th percentile is the value at the 8208th position (95% of 8640). The top 5% of spikes are discarded.

Strategy:
- If you burst traffic to high peaks (>95th percentile), they're discarded and don't count
- But sustained utilization near the 95th percentile costs you
- Use traffic shaping to cap bursts that exceed the 95th percentile level
- Schedule non-critical traffic to avoid shaping during peak hours

Example: If your 95th percentile is 80 Mbps (billed level), short spikes to 120 Mbps don't increase cost. But sustained usage at 90 Mbps does — you'll be billed at 90 Mbps next month.

Action: Shape non-critical traffic to keep sustained utilization near the desired billing level.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• Capacity planning monitors current utilization, trends growth, and forecasts upgrade timing
• Key thresholds: 70% (watch), 80% (plan), 90% (act immediately)
• Always include procurement lead time (30-90 days) in upgrade planning
• Use 95th percentile for sustained peak analysis (discards top 5% of spikes)
• Monthly review, quarterly reporting, 5-year hardware refresh cycle
• Account for seasonal patterns and asymmetric traffic (download > upload)

**Best Practice:** Automate capacity monitoring with SNMP polling (5-minute intervals) and graphing (Grafana, Cacti, PRTG). Set up alerts for 70/80/90% thresholds. Document capacity plans in a shared location with budget estimates. Review plans with management quarterly to align with business growth projections.
